description: Traits. Observer descriptions are 'documented' as observations; generalisations are 'inferred'.

evidence_levels.documented: stated in a cited source (Verne's reported words, firsthand observation, or reliable reference)
evidence_levels.inferred: reasoned from multiple sources; see reasoning
evidence_levels.speculative: plausible but weakly or not supported by collected sources

records.claim: Appeared reluctant to talk about himself or his books; interviewers needed his wife's help to draw him out.

citations.quote: M. Verne is singularly modest about his work, and showed no desire to talk about either his books or himself

records.claim: A slow, meticulous reviser who claimed never to have done slovenly work and corrected 7-9 sets of proofs.

citations.quote: I am never satisfied with less than seven or eight proofs
I don’t think I have ever done a piece of slovenly work
I often have as many as eight or nine revises

records.topic: wounded pride / desire for literary recognition
records.claim: Felt deeply that French literary establishment ignored him and wanted recognition as a stylist and artist, more than money or decorations.
records.caveats: Sherard's interview is Verne's speech as reported/translated by a journalist; some dates in it are wrong (e.g. Five Weeks is dated 1861 and Verne's age at writing as 25; actual publication Jan 1863, Verne aged 34).

citations.quote: great regret of my life is that I have never taken any place in French literature
I am an artist

records.claim: Contemporaries described him as genial, good-hearted, without enemies or literary jealousy.

citations.quote: an aroma of goodness and kindness of heart
ni jalousie ni petitesse, rien des mesquines passions du rival de lettres

records.claim: Combined a Parisian boulevardier's gaiety with a love of solitude and quiet; Verne himself said he could be happiest 'in a cloister'.

citations.quote: gai causeur, inventeur inépuisable, boulevardier et solitaire
could never be happier than in a cloister

records.claim: Rigid routine: rose ~5 am, wrote until 11, read periodicals in the afternoon, asleep by 8-8:30 pm.

citations.quote: I rise every morning before five
each evening he is generally sound asleep by eight

records.claim: Spoke rapidly with quick hand movements; energetic manner even at 61.

citations.quote: M. Verne spoke in a short, rapid way
the rapidity of his speech and the quick movements of his firm white hands

records.claim: Worked in a tiny, bare, cell-like room with a camp bed; extremely neat desk and manuscript.

citations.quote: The room was very small
a tiny, cell-like bed-chamber

records.claim: Lost interest in a book once proofs were done; never re-read his stories (per his wife), though he once jokingly said he read 'a novel by Jules Verne' with enjoyment.
records.caveats: The two statements conflict mildly; the second is likely playful.

citations.quote: has never re-read a chapter of a single one of his stories
pick up a novel by Jules Verne and read it with enjoyment

records.claim: Presented himself as no 'money-getting man' despite feeling underpaid by early contracts.
records.caveats: Self-presentation; Hetzel correspondence (not collected) shows he negotiated actively.

citations.quote: But I am not and never have been a money-getting man

records.claim: A smiling melancholy, especially in later life (regret over recognition, loss of travel).
records.reasoning: Claretie (1883) already notes 'mélancolie souriante'; Sherard (1893) records sadness about literary standing; Belloc records him 'half sadly' saying he now travels only in imagination. Consistent across three observers.

citations.quote: l’espèce de mélancolie souriante du marin
I now journey only in imagination

records.claim: Playful, gallant humour with women visitors and his wife.

citations.quote: You may save a young widower before you return
with a charming air of old-fashioned gallantry
